sentence: The NHS describes migraine as a set of symptoms, not just a headache.
note: NHS: 'a set of symptoms that often includes...'

sentence: These often include a throbbing headache on one side of the head, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound.
Other symptoms can include feeling very tired, craving certain foods, mood changes, a stiff neck and needing to pass urine more often.
note: NHS summary list of other common symptoms

sentence: Some people get an aura before the headache.
An aura can involve sight problems such as zigzag lines or flashing lights, or pins-and-needles numbness.
An aura appears gradually over a number of minutes and generally lasts less than an hour.
note: Summary quoted this wording; page attribution between Migraine Trust aura page and PMC review not certain

sentence: An attack can pass through several phases.
note: Summary of phases from NINDS/StatPearls results

sentence: Early warning symptoms can appear hours to a day or two before an attack.
note: 'Premonitory symptoms occur hours to a day or two before a migraine attack'

sentence: After the headache settles, lingering symptoms may last up to two days before a person feels healthy again.
note: 'The postdrome phase may last up to two days before people feel healthy again'; page attribution uncertain

sentence: Not every phase occurs in every attack.
Migraine without aura is the most common form, making up about three quarters of cases in one review.
note: 'accounting for 75% of cases'; attribution between the two ncbi pages uncertain

sentence: Migraine with aura has several subtypes.
Typical aura involves changes in vision, other sensory symptoms such as tingling, or problems with speaking.
note: 'changes in their vision, other symptoms affecting their senses (like tingles), or problems with speaking'

sentence: Brainstem aura includes at least two symptoms during an episode, such as vertigo, double vision, balance trouble or slurred speech.
Some people have aura symptoms but no headache, which is sometimes called silent migraine.
note: 'aura symptoms but don't get a headache... silent migraine'

sentence: Hemiplegic migraine is a rare type that involves temporary weakness or paralysis on one side of the body.
note: 'rare type of migraine involving temporary weakness or paralysis on one side'

sentence: It can run in families or occur without a family history.
note: Summary said familial or sporadic; attribution not certain

sentence: Vestibular migraine is migraine with dizziness, unsteadiness or vertigo, and is sometimes called migrainous vertigo.
Chronic migraine means migraine headaches on at least 15 days of the month for more than three months, with or without aura.
note: 'at least 15 days of the month for more than three months'

sentence: NICE advises a headache diary, kept for a minimum of eight weeks, recording how often headaches happen, how long and how severe they are, other symptoms and all medicines taken.
For migraine linked to periods, a diary covering at least the next two periods is advised.
A secondary headache is one caused by another problem.
NICE says a GP may refer for tests or to a specialist if a secondary cause is suspected.
Examples include a head injury within the past three months, headaches that start very suddenly, and problems with speech or balance that happen regularly and are getting worse.
People with tension-type headache or migraine are not referred for imaging if they have no signs or symptoms of a secondary headache.
The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help manage attacks and prevent them.
Options for attacks include painkillers such as ibuprofen and paracetamol, triptans, gepants and medicines for nausea.
Gepants are a newer class, and a Scottish NHS pathway says the gepant rimegepant can be considered when triptans have failed or cannot be used.
The Migraine Trust says gepants do not appear to cause medication overuse headache, while triptans and painkillers can.
The NHS lists preventive options including beta blockers, antidepressants and medicines for epilepsy.
It also lists acupuncture, relaxation techniques, cognitive behavioural therapy and vitamin B2.
A Scottish pathway also names candesartan, CGRP antibodies, flunarizine and botulinum toxin.
In the UK, CGRP antibodies, gepants and flunarizine are generally prescribed by headache specialists rather than GPs.
Medication overuse headache is a pattern in which headaches keep coming back because of frequent use of pain medicines.
note: NHS summary: rebound headaches due to overuse

sentence: The Migraine Trust says painkillers, ibuprofen, triptans and opioids can trigger it.
The Migraine Trust says attacks usually result from several factors together rather than one trigger alone.
It lists skipped meals, poor sleep and high stress as common contributors.
The NHS says avoiding known triggers may reduce attacks, and that eating and sleeping well and regular exercise can also help.
Keeping a diary may help a person notice patterns, with entries such as sleep, meals, caffeine, alcohol, stress, weather and the menstrual cycle.
The Trust cautions that cutting out foods or drinks believed to be triggers may not lead to fewer attacks.
Regular bedtimes and wake times are recommended, since too little and too much sleep can each trigger attacks in some people.
Intense exercise can trigger attacks in some people, but regular exercise at a manageable level can be positive for most.
Stress is a common trigger, and the Trust describes a let-down attack that happens when stress falls away.
The NHS says to call 999 for a sudden, extremely painful headache, trouble speaking, loss of vision, confusion, a seizure, or weakness on one side of the body.
Urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP the same day is advised if an attack has lasted longer than 72 hours, if an aura lasts longer than an hour, or if the person is pregnant or has just had a baby.
A routine GP appointment is advised if headaches keep happening or are not controlled by treatment.
The NHS says a GP may refer someone to a neurologist, a doctor who specialises in the brain and nerves, if the diagnosis is unclear or attacks are not controlled by current treatment.
